newsitem.title: USA: U.S. closer to decision on Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. closer to decision on Zaire crisis.

text.p: The United States, under growing pressure to take action in Zaire's refugee crisis, on Tuesday inched closer to a decision on whether to support a proposal to send a multinational force to the region.

A military-led U.S. assessment team has been sent to the region, and officials hinted that President Bill Clinton would approve Canadian leadership of the multinational force. Many international leaders have said such a force is essential to avoid a refugee disaster.

But White House and State Department spokesmen said Clinton still had not made a decision on whether to back a multinational force or whether Washington would play any role, such as contributing troops.
The proposed force's mission would be to aid starving refugees in eastern Zaire who have been fleeing fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zaire's army.

Officials also continued to leave open the door to U.S. logistics support for the mission and for some ground troops. Talks have focused on a few thousand American troops being part of the multinational force, officials said.
A formal U.S. decision could come as early as Wednesday, officials and diplomats said.

"It's (Canadian leadership proposal) on the table. It's in play. It's something we're actively considering," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, accompanying Secretary of State Warren Christopher to a Bosnia conference in Paris.
A senior U.S. official, referring to a published report that Washington rejected Canadian leadership of the force, said: "I would lead you in the opposite direction."

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali told a news conference in Rome that Canada had agreed to lead a force of troops from more than 12 countries, and he hoped the Security Council would approve a mandate in the next few days.
France, meanwhile, stepped up criticism of the United States for dragging its feet over joining the force.
The latest blast by Defence Minister Charles Millon came on the eve of a visit to Paris by Christopher.

In Ottawa, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien urged quick U.N. approval and said the first Canadian troops could be deployed within 48 hours of getting the go-ahead. Chretien planned to call Clinton later to discuss the issue.

Senior Canadian officials and the former chief U.N. military adviser, Lt. Gen. Joseph Maurice Baril -- who Canada is recommending to head the Zaire force -- were in Washington on Tuesday meeting National Security Council adviser Anthony Lake and other officials.

U.S. officials said the U.S. assessment team, headed by U.S. Army Maj. Gen. Edward Smith, commander of the South European Task Force based in Vicenza, Italy, would arrive in Central Africa on Wednesday to examine the situation.

The Pentagon said the military investigation team, totalling about 40 people, would include one representative each from Britain, France and Canada. The team is expected to arrive in the region on Wednesday but its itinerary is not yet set.

Asked if the team represented a U.S. commitment to deploy forces in Central Africa, Army Lt. Col. Nancy Burt, a Pentagon spokeswoman, said: "The deployment of this team enhances the military's ability to respond but does not represent a commitment by the U.S. to deploy other forces."
State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said the complexity of the Zaire humanitarian crisis and the need for a solution that "makes sense" was holding up the U.S. decision.
He also told reporters repatriating the refugees to Rwanda must be part of an international solution to the crisis.
The mix of militias, ethnic groups and refugees on Zaire's border with Rwanda made for a "very complex situation," more so than most humanitarian crises, he said.

"And the essence of it for the United States is deciding what makes sense to do, what can we do, and then to make a decision whether or not to go ahead and do that. I mean that decision has yet to be made," he said.

He added: "The challenge ... the puzzle ... (is) putting together something that will work, that will take best advantage of what the various players can bring to the mission ... And it's not simply a question of parachuting in foodstuffs or water to people because in this situation... we're not even sure where the people are."

The United States has said a force is needed but, remembering a U.N. mission to Somalia in 1993 which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other troops, has insisted on seeing full details of the force's mandate and funding.

Most of the refugees in eastern Zaire are Rwandan Hutus who fled Rwanda in 1994 when rebels of the Tutsi minority ousted the Hutu-dominated government which had orchestrated the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
